quests.hint: Use 'I usually…' with the simple present to describe your regular morning habits.
quests.explanation: 'I usually' is the key phrase for routines. The simple present tense ('I wake up, I make coffee') is the correct form for habits and repeated actions in English.
quests.situationText: Your language partner asks what your typical weekday morning routine looks like before work.
quests.sampleAnswer: I usually wake up at six thirty, have a quick shower, grab a coffee, and catch the seven fifteen bus. Very routine but it works!

quests.hint: Use 'In the evenings, I tend to…' to describe what you do most evenings naturally.
quests.explanation: 'I tend to' is softer and more natural than 'I always.' It implies something you do most of the time - which is more honest and sounds more fluent than claiming a rigid, never-changing schedule.
quests.situationText: A classmate asks what you normally do in the evenings after school or work.
quests.sampleAnswer: In the evenings I tend to cook something simple, watch a series for an hour, and then read before bed. Pretty quiet but I like it!
quests.correctAnswer: cook something simple in the evenings
acceptedSynonyms: cook something simple in the evenings
in the evenings I tend to

quests.hint: Use 'On weekday mornings I have to…' to describe obligatory parts of your routine.
quests.explanation: 'I have to' correctly describes external obligations. This separates things you must do (commute, prepare children for school) from things you choose to do, making your description more precise.
quests.situationText: Someone asks how your weekday mornings compare with your much more relaxed weekend mornings.
quests.sampleAnswer: On weekday mornings I have to be out the door by seven thirty sharp. Weekends I don't set an alarm at all - it's bliss!
quests.correctAnswer: out the door by seven thirty
acceptedSynonyms: out the door by seven thirty
weekdays I do not set an alarm

quests.hint: Use 'For breakfast I usually have…' to describe your morning meal simply and naturally.
quests.explanation: 'For breakfast I usually have toast and eggs' is a clear, natural sentence structure. Using 'for' with meal names is standard in English: 'for breakfast', 'for lunch', 'for dinner.'
quests.situationText: Your new English friend is curious about what people typically eat for breakfast in your country.
quests.sampleAnswer: For breakfast I usually have rice porridge or eggs on toast. Back home, a hot breakfast is considered really important every day!

quests.hint: Use 'I'm in the mood for…' to express what kind of food you feel like eating right now.
quests.explanation: 'I'm in the mood for' is a natural, idiomatic phrase describing a current food craving. It is far more expressive and natural than simply saying 'I want to eat pizza tonight.'
quests.situationText: Your friend asks you what you feel like having for dinner tonight. You have a strong craving.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm really in the mood for Thai food tonight. There's that great place near the station - shall we try it?
acceptedSynonyms: in the mood for something spicy

quests.hint: Use 'My favourite dish is… because…' to talk about a food you love and give a genuine reason.
quests.explanation: Giving a reason ('because') transforms a simple statement into an interesting conversation. 'My favourite dish is my grandmother's soup because it reminds me of home' invites the listener to share their own.
quests.situationText: An English colleague asks you what your all-time favourite meal or dish is and why you love it.
quests.sampleAnswer: My favourite dish is slow-cooked lamb tagine because the spices are incredible and it reminds me of my mother's cooking. Nothing beats it.

quests.hint: Use 'In my free time I enjoy…' followed by a verb+ing to describe your hobbies grammatically.
quests.explanation: 'I enjoy + verb-ing' is the grammatically correct structure in English. 'I enjoy to swim' is incorrect; 'I enjoy swimming' is right. This verb+ing pattern applies after all 'enjoy', 'love', 'hate', 'avoid.'
quests.situationText: Someone at your new English class asks what hobbies you have in your free time.
quests.sampleAnswer: In my free time I enjoy hiking and amateur photography. I try to get outdoors at least once every weekend if the weather allows.
acceptedSynonyms: in my free time I enjoy

quests.hint: Use 'I've been [doing activity] for [time period]' to describe how long you have had a hobby.
quests.explanation: 'I've been playing guitar for five years' uses present perfect continuous - the correct tense for activities that started in the past and continue now. This is an important and commonly tested grammar point.
quests.situationText: Your teacher asks the class how long each student has been doing their main hobby.
quests.sampleAnswer: I've been doing watercolour painting for about three years. I started during lockdown and completely fell in love with it.
acceptedSynonyms: completely fell in love with it

quests.hint: Use 'You should try…' to make an enthusiastic, friendly hobby recommendation.
quests.explanation: 'You should try rock climbing' is a natural, encouraging recommendation. Adding 'you'd love it' expresses confident belief that the other person would enjoy the activity - it turns advice into an invitation.
quests.situationText: Your friend says they want to find an exciting new hobby and asks for a personal suggestion.
quests.sampleAnswer: You should try indoor rock climbing! You'd absolutely love it - it's a full-body workout and it's incredibly satisfying when you reach the top.

quests.hint: Use 'It's absolutely boiling!' or 'It's roasting out there!' for very hot weather in informal English.
quests.explanation: 'It's boiling' and 'It's roasting' are common hyperbolic English expressions for extreme heat. They go well beyond the literal meaning and show confident, natural use of informal vocabulary.
quests.situationText: You bump into a neighbour on the street on the hottest day of the summer so far.
quests.sampleAnswer: Isn't it absolutely boiling today?! I've never been so relieved to get back indoors in my life. Extraordinary heat!

quests.hint: Use 'It looks like rain' or 'It's supposed to be sunny later' to talk about predicted weather.
quests.explanation: 'It looks like rain' uses 'looks like' for a visual prediction. 'It's supposed to be' refers to a forecast. Both are natural phrases English speakers use frequently throughout their day.
quests.situationText: A colleague peeks out the office window before lunch and asks what the weather looks like.
quests.sampleAnswer: It looks like it might rain this afternoon - the sky's gone quite grey. I'd take an umbrella just in case if I were you.

quests.hint: Comment on beautiful weather with 'What a gorgeous day!' or 'It's stunning out there, isn't it?'
quests.explanation: 'What a gorgeous day!' is a classic English exclamation for beautiful weather. The tag question 'isn't it?' invites the other person to agree and continue chatting - a very British conversational habit.
quests.situationText: You step outside on a perfect spring morning and it is warm, sunny, and completely beautiful.
quests.sampleAnswer: What an absolutely gorgeous morning! This is the kind of weather that makes you want to ditch everything and spend the day outside.

quests.hint: Ask 'Do you have this in a medium/large?' - always name the item AND the size you need.
quests.explanation: Naming both the item and your size ('Do you have this jumper in a medium?') gives the shop assistant all the information they need immediately. This avoids follow-up questions and speeds up service considerably.
quests.situationText: You find a jumper you love but only small sizes seem to be left on the rack.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, do you have this blue jumper in a medium? I can only seem to find small sizes on the rack here.
quests.correctAnswer: do you have this in a medium
acceptedSynonyms: do you have this in a medium

quests.hint: Say 'I'd like to try this on, please' or 'Could I try this on?' before heading to the fitting room.
quests.explanation: 'I'd like to try this on' is the standard phrase for trying on clothes. It is direct but polite. In most shops, you can go directly to fitting rooms, but informing staff shows good manners.
quests.situationText: You have found a dress you like and want to see how it fits before making any decision.
quests.sampleAnswer: Could I try this dress on, please? I'd like to see how it fits before I decide whether to buy it.

quests.hint: When returning an item, say 'I'd like to return this' and clearly give your reason.
quests.explanation: 'I'd like to return this' is polite and direct. Giving your reason ('it doesn't fit', 'it was a gift in the wrong size') helps staff process the return efficiently and professionally.
quests.situationText: You bought a coat last week but it is one size too small and does not fit properly at all.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, I'd like to return this coat please. I bought it on Saturday but it's unfortunately a size too small for me.

quests.hint: Use 'We have a reservation for [number] under the name [name]' when arriving at a restaurant.
quests.explanation: Stating your reservation details clearly ('a table for two under Johnson') is efficient and professional. It helps the host find your booking immediately and creates a smooth, confident check-in.
quests.situationText: You arrive at a smart restaurant for a birthday dinner and approach the reception desk.
quests.sampleAnswer: Good evening! We have a reservation for four people at seven thirty. It's under the name Patel.
quests.correctAnswer: reservation for four at seven thirty
acceptedSynonyms: reservation for four at seven thirty

quests.hint: Say 'I'll go for the…' or 'I'll have the…' when ordering from a menu to sound natural.
quests.explanation: 'I'll go for the salmon' and 'I'll have the pasta' are both very natural ordering phrases. They signal a confident decision. Avoid 'I want the…' in formal restaurant settings as it can sound slightly demanding.
quests.situationText: The waiter returns with a notepad and asks if you have decided what you would like for dinner.
quests.sampleAnswer: For my starter I'll have the soup, and for my main I'll go for the roasted duck, please. Thank you!
quests.correctAnswer: soup for my starter and the roasted duck
acceptedSynonyms: soup for my starter and the roasted duck

quests.hint: Flag a problem politely: 'Excuse me, I think there might be an issue with my order.'
quests.explanation: 'I think there might be an issue with my order' is non-accusatory and professional. Using 'might be' softens the statement and avoids sounding aggressive or rude to a server who may not be at fault.
quests.situationText: Your food arrives but it is the completely wrong dish - you ordered fish but received chicken.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, I think there might be a mix-up with my order. I ordered the sea bass but this looks like the chicken. Could you check?

quests.hint: Ask 'Does this bus go to…?' to confirm a route before boarding.
quests.explanation: 'Does this bus go to the city centre?' prevents taking the wrong bus - one of the most common travel mistakes. Asking before boarding is the sensible English approach to public transport navigation.
quests.situationText: You see a bus approaching the stop and are unsure if it goes in the direction you need.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, does this bus go to the main train station? I'm not entirely sure I'm at the right stop here.
quests.correctAnswer: does this bus go to the train station
acceptedSynonyms: does this bus go to the train station

quests.hint: Buy a ticket with 'Can I have a single/return to [destination], please?'
quests.explanation: 'A single' means a one-way ticket; 'a return' means round trip. These are the standard British English ticket phrases - essential vocabulary for confident travel on UK trains and buses.
quests.situationText: You are at the ticket counter at a train station and need to buy a ticket to your destination.
quests.sampleAnswer: Could I have a return ticket to Cambridge, please? And can you tell me which platform the next train leaves from?

quests.hint: Offer your seat with 'Would you like to sit down?' - polite and considerate on public transport.
quests.explanation: 'Would you like to sit down?' is a gentle, polite offer of your seat. Using 'would you like' is more gracious than simply pointing at the seat - it gives the person the genuine choice to accept or decline.
quests.situationText: An older woman with heavy shopping bags is standing near you on a packed bus.
quests.sampleAnswer: Please, would you like my seat? I'm getting off at the next stop in just a couple of minutes.
acceptedSynonyms: getting off at the next stop

quests.hint: Use 'I'm not feeling very well' or 'I feel a bit under the weather' to say you are ill politely.
quests.explanation: 'Not feeling very well' is a polite understatement for illness. 'Under the weather' is a common English idiom for feeling mildly unwell. Both are used constantly in everyday English interactions.
quests.situationText: You arrive at school looking pale and your teacher notices immediately and comes to check on you.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm really not feeling very well today, honestly. I think I've got some kind of stomach bug. I'm so sorry.
quests.correctAnswer: come down with a stomach bug
acceptedSynonyms: come down with a stomach bug

quests.hint: Describe symptoms using 'I've got a [symptom]' or 'My [body part] is [adjective].'
quests.explanation: 'I've got a headache' and 'My throat is really sore' are natural English symptom descriptions. 'I've got' (British English) and 'I have' (American English) are both correct for describing ailments to a doctor.
quests.situationText: The doctor asks you to describe the symptoms that brought you in to the surgery today.
quests.sampleAnswer: I've got a really sore throat and a slight fever. My head is pounding behind my eyes too. It all started two days ago.
quests.correctAnswer: sore throat and a slight fever
acceptedSynonyms: sore throat and a slight fever

quests.hint: Call in sick with 'I'm afraid I won't be able to come in today because…'
quests.explanation: 'I'm afraid I won't be able to come in today' is the professional, polite formula for calling in sick. 'I'm afraid' is a common English phrase for softening disappointing news in a formal context.
quests.situationText: You need to call your manager early this morning to explain you cannot come into work today.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, it's James. I'm afraid I won't be able to come in today - I have a high fever and my doctor has told me to rest.
quests.correctAnswer: high fever and doctor has advised me to rest
acceptedSynonyms: high fever and doctor has advised me to rest
won't be able to come in today

quests.hint: Use 'I work as a…' or 'I'm a [job title] at [company]' to describe your profession naturally.
quests.explanation: 'I work as a teacher at a secondary school' is natural and professional. Both 'I work as' and 'I am a' are correct, but 'I work as' emphasizes the role you perform.
quests.situationText: At a social event someone you have just met asks what you do for a living.
quests.sampleAnswer: I work as a graphic designer at a small creative agency. It's varied and I really enjoy the problem-solving side of it.
quests.correctAnswer: graphic designer at a creative agency
acceptedSynonyms: graphic designer at a creative agency

quests.hint: Use 'I'm studying [subject] at [institution]' to describe your studies with the right tense.
quests.explanation: 'I'm studying' uses present continuous - the correct tense for an ongoing study programme. Adding the institution makes the description more complete and gives the listener context.
quests.situationText: A new person at your language exchange evening asks what you are currently studying.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm studying civil engineering at the university here. I'm in my final year and honestly I can't wait to graduate!

quests.hint: Use 'My hours are…' or 'I work from… to…' to describe your working schedule clearly.
quests.explanation: Describing working hours ('I work from nine to five' or 'I have flexible hours') gives a complete picture of your schedule. This is a very common topic in English social conversation and job interviews.
quests.situationText: A classmate asks you about the part-time job you mentioned - specifically what hours you work.
quests.sampleAnswer: I work Monday, Wednesday, and Friday evenings from five until nine. Part-time suits me perfectly while I'm still studying.

quests.hint: Use 'What did you get up to this weekend?' to ask what someone did last weekend in informal English.
quests.explanation: 'What did you get up to?' is natural and informal - 'get up to' is a phrasal verb meaning 'do' or 'be involved in,' widely used in British English. It is much more natural than 'What did you do?'
quests.situationText: It is Monday morning and you want to ask your colleague about their weekend in a friendly way.
quests.sampleAnswer: How was your weekend? What did you get up to? Did you manage to do anything nice or was it mostly relaxing?
acceptedSynonyms: what did you get up to

quests.hint: Share what you did using 'I ended up…' for something spontaneous or unexpected that happened.
quests.explanation: 'I ended up going to a concert' suggests something that happened perhaps spontaneously or differently from the original plan. This phrase makes past-tense storytelling feel natural, vivid, and engaging.
quests.situationText: Your friend asks what you did last weekend. You went to a concert completely spontaneously.
quests.sampleAnswer: I ended up going to a last-minute outdoor concert on Saturday - it was absolutely brilliant. Completely unplanned but one of the best nights I've had in ages!

quests.hint: Use 'I'm planning to…' for decided future plans and 'I'm thinking of…' for more tentative ones.
quests.explanation: 'I'm planning to' suggests a firm decision; 'I'm thinking of' is more tentative. Both are grammatically correct for near-future plans. Choosing between them shows precision in English.
quests.situationText: A colleague asks what your plans are for the coming weekend - anything exciting on the horizon.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm planning to visit some old friends on Saturday, and on Sunday I'm thinking of going for a long hike if the forecast is decent.
quests.correctAnswer: old friends on Saturday and a hike on Sunday
acceptedSynonyms: old friends on Saturday and a hike on Sunday
